issues.claim: adopted 18 December 2024
issues.source_says: Cover page: 'Adopted on 17 December 2024'. 18 December is the publication date, not the adoption date.

issues.claim: anonymous only where identification of individuals or extraction of their data through queries is very unlikely
issues.source_says: Para 43 (p. 15) and executive summary: both the likelihood of direct (including probabilistic) extraction of personal data of individuals whose data were used to train the model, and the likelihood of obtaining such data from queries, should be 'insignificant', taking into account all means reasonably likely to be used. 'Very unlikely' is a loose paraphrase of 'insignificant'.

issues.claim: governs the data side that Article 2(7) leaves to the GDPR
issues.source_says: The Opinion does not cite Article 2(7) AI Act. It refers to the AI Act only for definitions (Art. 3(1), Recital 97), Art. 10(5), Art. 5(1)-(2) and the EU declaration of conformity (Arts 16(g), 47), and says in para 117 that SA measures under the GDPR are without prejudice to those taken under the AI Act.

proposed_takeaway: Article 64(2) GDPR opinion adopted 17 December 2024 and published the next day, at the request of the Irish supervisory authority. It holds that an AI model trained on personal data is anonymous only where the likelihood of extracting individuals' data from the model or obtaining it through queries is insignificant, assessed case by case; sets a three-step test for legitimate interest in training and deployment, with conversational agents and threat detection as acceptable purposes when strictly necessary and balanced; and warns that models built on unlawfully processed data may face corrective measures and restrictions on subsequent use unless properly anonymised. It does not implement the AI Act but governs the data side that Article 2(7) leaves to the GDPR.
note: Substance confirmed (Irish SA request, case-by-case anonymity, three-step test, three unlawful-processing scenarios); only the adoption date and the anonymity threshold wording need tightening.

issues.claim: asked that data protection authorities be the national supervisory authorities and the EDPS the authority for Union institutions
issues.source_says: Executive summary (p. 3) and paras 47-53: the Commission proposal already designated the EDPS as competent authority and market surveillance authority for Union institutions; the EDPB and EDPS 'welcome' that designation and ask that its role be clarified. The request they made was that DPAs be designated national supervisory authorities under Article 59 of the Proposal.

proposed_takeaway: Joint opinion of 18 June 2021 on the Commission's April 2021 proposal, now legislative history. The two bodies called for a general ban on any use of AI for automated recognition of human features in publicly accessible spaces, a ban on social scoring, a ban on inferring emotions except for narrow cases and a ban on biometric categorisation by protected characteristics, asked that data protection authorities be the national supervisory authorities and welcomed the EDPS as the authority for Union institutions. The enacted Article 5 adopted narrower prohibitions. Read it to understand why DPAs still press for a fundamental-rights reading of the Act.
note: Date, proposal date (21 April 2021), the four bans (emotion inference excepted for health or research) and the DPA request all confirmed; the enacted Article 5 comparison is outside the document.

issues.claim: Adopted at the 8 July 2026 plenary
issues.source_says: Cover page and version history: 'Version 1.0, Adopted on 07 July 2026, adoption of the guidelines for public consultation'.

issues.claim: for public consultation until 30 October 2026
issues.source_says: The text confirms adoption for public consultation but gives no closing date; the deadline is not in the document.

issues.claim: require ... accuracy with timestamping and validation
issues.source_says: Executive summary (p. 3) and para on accuracy (p. 12): 'it is recommended that the controller scrape from reliable sources, timestamp the data and validate the data before using them in AI training'. Recommended measures, not requirements.

issues.claim: They complement the copyright policy and training-content summary duties in Article 53
issues.source_says: The guidelines do not cite the AI Act or Article 53; copyright appears only as a mitigating measure referencing Directive 2019/790 (p. 18).

proposed_takeaway: Adopted on 7 July 2026 for public consultation until 30 October 2026. The guidelines confirm that the GDPR applies to collection, storage, organisation and retrieval of scraped personal data, require purpose limitation, transparency and minimisation, recommend timestamping and validation for accuracy, clarify legitimate interest as the basis for training, and require both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9 exception for special-category data, citing GC and Others (C-136/17) for incidental collection with safeguards. They complement the copyright policy and training-content summary duties in Article 53. Providers scraping for training should align data governance with them now, before the final version.
note: Document title is 'Guidelines 03/2026 on web scraping in the context of generative AI'; the blockchain files on the same page were ignored as instructed.

None of the three files is Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation: they are the web scraping guidelines 03/2026, blockchain guidelines 02/2025 v2.0 and the blockchain consultation report. The anonymisation guidelines PDF was not downloaded from the news page.

issues.claim: the origin of the positions later formalised in Opinion 28/2024 and the 2026 web-scraping guidelines
issues.source_says: A statement about later documents; not addressed in the report itself.

note: Date 23 May 2024, taskforce set up 13 April 2023, preliminary views on lawfulness (web scraping, Art. 6(1)(f) with safeguards), fairness, transparency (Art. 14), accuracy and data subject rights, and OSS applying from the 15 February 2024 Irish establishment all confirmed.

issues.claim: a first layer that names every purpose, identifies the controllers behind consent-requiring trackers
issues.source_says: Purposes on the first screen is confirmed (para 14, p.4). For controllers, paras 18 to 21 (p.6) require that users can know the identity of all controllers before choosing, but say the specific information may be given at a second level reached from the first level by a link or button; only the number of controllers 'could' be shown at the first level.

issues.claim: is the reference the CNIL uses in its cookie fines
issues.source_says: Not addressed by the recommendation. Para 3 (p.2) states the text is neither prescriptive nor exhaustive and other consent methods may be used.

issues.claim: It applies to sites and apps subject to the 2020 guidelines
issues.source_says: Para 5 (p.2): it concerns all organisations using trackers as defined in the guidelines of 17 September 2020; para 6 says it particularly covers web and mobile apps but the examples can guide other contexts (connected TV, consoles, voice assistants).

proposed_takeaway: The recommendation gives the CNIL's expected banner design: a first layer that names every purpose, gives access to the full list of controllers behind consent-requiring trackers, and offers an accept action and a refuse action of equal effort, with a refusal remembered so that the user is not asked again at each visit. It applies to every organisation using trackers as defined in the 2020 guidelines, web and mobile first, and is the reference the CNIL uses in its cookie fines. Build banners to it, log consent and refusal, and re-ask no more often than the recommended six-month rhythm.
note: Deliberation number, date, equal-effort refusal (paras 30 to 34), retention of choices and six-month good practice (paras 37 to 39) and proof of consent (para 46) all confirmed.

issues.claim: first published on 24 September 2024
issues.source_says: Cover page (p.1) and the annotated version say the initial recommendation was adopted on 18 July 2024 by Deliberation 2024-061, which Deliberation 2025-024 repeals; no September 2024 publication date appears in the text.

issues.claim: The 2025 amendments are non-substantive corrections and clarifications requested by stakeholders
issues.source_says: The text does not characterise the amendments or mention stakeholder requests. The annotated version (recommandation-applications-mobiles-modifiee_suivi.txt) shows targeted edits: typo and footnote fixes, but also a change to the qualification of publisher and SDK provider in the location-SDK example and an added passage on SDK providers processing data for their own account (section 4.2).

issues.claim: the CNIL's announced app inspections
issues.source_says: No inspection campaign is mentioned in the recommendation.

proposed_takeaway: The recommendation, first adopted on 18 July 2024 (Deliberation 2024-061) and replaced by the amended version adopted in Deliberation 2025-024 of 27 March 2025 and published on 8 April 2025, sets the CNIL's expectations for each actor in the mobile chain (publisher, developer, SDK provider, operating system and store), including how consent for trackers and permissions must be collected in-app under article 82 and the GDPR. The 2025 amendments are targeted corrections and clarifications, shown in an annotated version, including the roles of publisher and SDK provider in one SDK example. Apps distributed in France should map SDKs against it and treat it as the yardstick for CNIL app inspections.
note: The two files of 326351 bytes are byte-identical (consolidated version); the third is the annotated track-changes version. Actors, article 82 basis and 8 April 2025 publication confirmed (pp.1, 5, 10).

issues.claim: affecting more than 74 million accounts and 53 million users respectively
issues.source_says: All account and user counts are redacted as [...] in the published decision (paras 6, 232, 236, 237), so the figures cannot be checked against it; they come from the CNIL's press material.

issues.claim: under a penalty of 100,000 euros per day each
issues.source_says: Operative part (p.54) and para 271 order a single penalty payment of 100,000 euros per day of delay after six months from notification, addressed to both companies; 'each' is not stated.

proposed_takeaway: The CNIL fined Google LLC 200 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 125 million euros for placing advertising cookies during Google account creation without valid, informed consent (article 82 of the French Data Protection Act) and for displaying adverts between emails in the Gmail Promotions and Social tabs without prior consent (article L.34-5 of the Postal and Electronic Communications Code), affecting more than 74 million accounts and 53 million users respectively. Both companies must comply within six months under a penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay. Account sign-up flows are cookie consent flows and the same banner standard applies.
note: SAN-2025-004 of 1 September 2025. Fines (paras 264, 265, p.52), article 82 finding (paras 153, 154), L.34-5 finding on Promotions and Social networks tabs (paras 187, 200) and six-month injunction confirmed.

issues.claim: the fine stands at the upper end of the CNIL's cookie sanctions
issues.source_says: The decision does not compare the fine with other CNIL cookie sanctions.

note: SAN-2025-005 of 1 September 2025: 150 million euros under article 82 (p.35), Irish company managing shein.com European subdomains (para 3), around 12 million unique visitors per month in France (para 167), cookies before consent, ineffective refusal and withdrawal (sections D.1 and D.2), banner and pop-up lacking advertising purposes and third-party identities (paras 107 to 121), no injunction because of compliance during the procedure (para 185) all confirmed.

issues.claim: with one exemption: measuring the individual deliverability of emails tied to a service the recipient asked for
issues.source_says: Section 3.2 (p.5) lists two exempted purposes: security measures contributing to user authentication, and individual measurement of open rates for deliverability, limited to what is strictly necessary to adapt or stop sending to inactive recipients. Both exemptions apply only to emails requested by the recipient or linked to a requested service.

issues.claim: consent to receive marketing does not exempt any other tracking purpose
issues.source_says: Section 4 (pp.9 to 10): the pixel consent regime is independent of the regime for sending the email, but a single consent may cover direct marketing under article L.34-5 CPCE together with pixel purposes connected to it (personalisation, sending frequency, anti-fraud in contests); distinct, unconnected purposes need separate consent.

issues.claim: Senders must clearly inform recipients about pixels and offer a simple way to object
issues.source_says: Section 5 (p.10): what is required for consent-based pixels is withdrawal of consent, as easy as giving it, for example through a per-recipient link in the footer of each email that works without re-entering the address. Objection is the route only for the transitional period in section 7.

issues.claim: published on 14 April 2026
issues.source_says: The text gives only 'Version adoptée le 12 mars 2026' (p.1); no publication date appears.

proposed_takeaway: The recommendation, adopted on 12 March 2026 and published on 14 April 2026, states that open-tracking pixels in emails require consent under article 82, with two exemptions: security measures that help authenticate the user, and measuring individual open rates for deliverability, limited to what is needed to adapt or stop sending to inactive recipients. Both exemptions cover only emails the recipient asked for or that relate to a service they requested, such as transactional messages (order confirmations, password resets, account alerts) and messages they consented to receive; pixel consent is separate from consent to receive the email itself, although one consent can cover direct marketing and the pixel purposes connected to it. Senders must clearly inform recipients about pixels and let them withdraw consent as easily as they gave it, for example through a footer link. For addresses collected before publication, senders had three months to inform recipients and give them an easy objection route. Email platforms and marketing teams should reconfigure open tracking to consent-gated operation.
note: Three-month transitional information duty (section 7, p.11) and transactional email examples (box on p.6) confirmed. The other three files are consultation summaries and an English version, not used.

issues.claim: It binds every information-society service targeting users in Spain
issues.source_says: Articles 2 to 4 (pp.8 to 9): the law applies to providers established in Spain, to non-EU/EEA providers that direct their services specifically at Spanish territory (article 4), and to providers established in another EU/EEA state only for the matters listed in article 3.1, which do not include article 22.2.

issues.claim: the AEPD enforces it as a leve or grave infringement depending on the breach
issues.source_says: Article 38.4.g classes a breach of article 22.2 as leve; it becomes grave only on recidivism declared by final decision within the previous three years (article 38.3.i). Article 43.1 gives the AEPD the power to sanction both.

proposed_takeaway: Article 22.2 LSSI allows a service provider to store or access information on a recipient's terminal only after the recipient has consented on the basis of clear and complete information about the purposes, exempts storage strictly necessary for transmission or for a service the user requested, and permits consent to be expressed through appropriate browser or application settings where technically possible. It binds providers established in Spain and non-EU providers that direct their services at Spain. The consolidated text was last updated on 23 January 2025 and the AEPD enforces it as a leve infringement, which becomes grave on repeat offences within three years.
note: Article 22.2 wording (p.17) and 'Última modificación: 23 de enero de 2025' confirmed.

issues.claim: large platforms cannot rely on a binary pay-or-consent choice and should offer a free alternative such as contextual advertising
issues.source_says: Section 3.2.10 (pp.29 to 30) reports Opinion 8/2024: in most cases large online platforms will not meet the conditions for valid consent if they offer only a binary choice, and they should consider offering an equivalent alternative without a fee, which could consist of general or contextual advertising.

issues.claim: It is the reference for AEPD sanction procedures in Spain
issues.source_says: The guide does not describe its own role in sanction procedures.

proposed_takeaway: The current guide applies article 22.2 LSSI together with the GDPR and LOPDGDD: a reject option must sit at the same layer and with the same visibility as accept, consent should be renewed at most every 24 months, cookie walls are lawful only with clear notice and a genuinely equivalent alternative that need not be free, and access to legally guaranteed rights cannot be blocked. A May 2024 section transposes EDPB Opinion 08/2024: large platforms will in most cases not obtain valid consent from a binary pay-or-consent choice and should consider a free alternative such as contextual advertising. It is the reference for AEPD sanction procedures in Spain.
note: Reject at same layer and level (pp.24, 26), 24-month good practice (section 3.2.8), cookie walls and legally recognised rights (section 3.2.10) confirmed.

issues.claim: omitted first-party and third-party detail and profiling purposes
issues.source_says: Proven facts (pp.1 to 2) and the AEPD's reasoning (pp.12 to 15): the first-layer banner was not concise, transparent or intelligible; the second layer did not identify third-party cookies or state retention periods. Omission of profiling purposes is not among the findings.

issues.claim: users could only accept or be denied access
issues.source_says: The cookie wall blocked browsing unless the user clicked accept or opened cookie settings; in settings cookies had to be refused group by group and a reject-all button only arrived in June 2020 (pp.2, 13).

issues.claim: loaded cookies automatically without acceptance
issues.source_says: Stated in the AEPD's request to Iberia of 29 November 2019 (p.1, cookies installed on visiting the home page), not restated among the proven facts of the decision.

issues.claim: A missing reject option alone reaches the top of the leve scale in Spain
issues.source_says: The 30,000 euro fine rests on several deficiencies (unclear first-layer information, cookie wall, no reject-all, missing third-party and retention information) plus the finding that Iberia did not meet any of the article 40 mitigation criteria (p.14).

proposed_takeaway: The AEPD imposed the maximum 30,000 euro fine for a leve infringement of article 22.2 LSSI under article 39.1.c because Iberia's banner used unclear wording, cookies were installed on the first visit, the second layer did not identify third-party cookies or their retention periods, and there was no genuine way to refuse: users could only accept or open the settings, where cookies had to be rejected group by group behind a cookie wall. The AEPD also found that the compliance changes Iberia claimed had not been implemented until after proceedings began, and confirmed the fine on reconsideration. A banner without an easy reject option reaches the top of the leve scale in Spain.
note: The file is the reconsideration decision (RR/582/2020) dismissing Iberia's appeal against the resolution of 16 October 2020; the 30,000 euro fine, article 22.2 basis, article 39.1.c ceiling (p.9) and late compliance finding (pp.12 to 15) confirmed. The 3 February 2021 date is not printed in the text.

issues.claim: Shopify, Klaviyo, Pinterest, Google and Meta cookies
issues.source_says: The decision lists only cookie names (_landing_page, _shopify_y, _shopify_s, __kla_id, _pin_unauth, test_cookie, IDE, _gcl_au, _fbp; pp.2, 5); the vendors are inferred from the names, not stated.

issues.claim: fined an online shop
issues.source_says: The website URL is redacted and the decision does not describe the company's business; the Shopify cookies imply a shop but the text does not say so.

note: Resolution of 18 January 2023: 5,000 euros under article 13 GDPR (privacy policy identifying the controller only by an email address) and 5,000 euros under article 22.2 LSSI (non-technical cookies set before any action, banner with only 'De acuerdo', no mechanism to reject or manage cookies); appeal dismissed (RR/00110/2023).

issues.claim: first adopted in December 2021 and revised by the 104th DSK in December 2022
issues.source_says: The text carries only 'ab dem 1. Dezember 2021', 'Version 1.1' and 'Stand: Dezember 2022' (p. 1); the 104th DSK appears only in the file name, not in the document, and the first version's adoption date is not stated.

issues.claim: German supervisory audits, including the BayLDA's, apply it
issues.source_says: Not addressed by the guidance itself (it is referenced in the BayLDA press release of 9 February 2024 in this packet).

note: Substantive claims confirmed: no personal data required (para 24, p. 9), economic necessity excluded (para 76, p. 28), Art. 6(1)(f) balancing cannot substitute for section 25(2) (para 67, pp. 22-23), reach measurement not per se necessary (paras 85-88, pp. 28-29), reject option must be an equivalent, first-layer alternative (paras 129-135, pp. 38-40).

issues.claim: Blanket consent covering several purposes is invalid
issues.source_says: Point 4: granular consent is required where purposes differ materially ('wesentlich voneinander abweichen'); bundling is possible only for purposes in a very close relationship; a blanket overall consent to such different purposes cannot be validly given.

issues.claim: should separate advertising, measurement and personalisation consents
issues.source_says: The Beschluss does not name these categories; it speaks generally of materially different purposes.

issues.claim: the EDPB's April 2024 opinion adds stricter conditions for large platforms
issues.source_says: Not in the document (dated 22 March 2023).

proposed_takeaway: The German authorities accept consent-or-pay (Pur-Abo) models on websites only where the paid alternative gives fundamentally the same service at a market-standard price, consent for the tracked version meets every GDPR requirement including granular consent per materially distinct purpose, and the paid version stores or reads only what is strictly necessary for the chosen service. Blanket consent covering materially different purposes is invalid; only closely related purposes may be bundled. Publishers using Pur-Abo models in Germany should separate advertising, measurement and personalisation consents and audit the paid path for tracking; the EDPB's April 2024 opinion adds stricter conditions for large platforms.
note: Date (22 March 2023), equivalence test, market-standard fee, section 25(1) TTDSG limit on the paid path and Art. 4(11)/7 requirements all confirmed.

issues.claim: Verwaltungsgericht Hannover, judgment 10 A 5385/22
issues.source_says: The only file is the DSK 'Orientierungshilfe fuer Anbieter:innen von digitalen Diensten (OH Digitale Dienste)', Version 1.2, Stand November 2024. It contains no reference to Hannover, 10 A 5385/22 or the LfD Niedersachsen order.

note: The LfD press page evidently linked the DSK OH Digitale Dienste rather than the judgment; the judgment text (or the press release) is needed to verify.

issues.claim: used an automated tool to check more than 350 Bavarian websites and 15 apps
issues.source_says: p. 1: a 'teils automatisierte' (partly automated) sweep of more than 350 websites and 15 apps; the automated tool was developed for cookie banners on websites, while app checks are described as still more laborious (manual).

issues.claim: the websites' banners failed the requirement
issues.source_says: p. 2: about 350 websites were picked up in the first run as not meeting the requirements; the tool initially targets one widely used CMP. Wording is acceptable but conflates the number examined with the number found wanting.

proposed_takeaway: The Bavarian State Office for Data Protection Supervision announced that in a partly automated sweep it had checked more than 350 Bavarian websites and 15 apps, finding that almost all apps ran consent-requiring processes before any consent and that about 350 websites failed the requirement, tested by its automated banner tool, that the option to withhold consent appear on the first layer alongside Accept all. Operators were given the opportunity to respond and fix their sites, and the BayLDA said it would extend the tool to further consent platforms. Expect scripted first-layer checks from German state authorities and design banners to pass them without human review.
note: Date 9 February 2024, counts, opportunity to respond and planned extension to further CMP providers all confirmed.

issues.claim: reliance on legitimate interest for non-essential cookies
issues.source_says: Not a finding against Roularta. The Inspection findings (pp. 3-5) and the operative findings (paras 162-163, pp. 51-53) are: non-essential cookies placed before consent; statistics cookies treated as not subject to consent and always active by default; pre-ticked partner boxes (Planet49); a disclaimer for third-party cookies (Arts 5(2), 24); deficient information (Arts 12-14); excessive cookie lifetimes (Art. 5(1)(e)); ineffective or impossible withdrawal (Art. 7(3)). Legitimate interest is mentioned once (para 89), as a reference to the earlier decision 12/2019.

issues.claim: In its first thematic investigation
issues.source_says: The decision records that the Comite de direction referred the media-site cookie file to the Inspection Service on 16 January 2019 (para 1) but does not call it the first thematic investigation.

issues.claim: A parallel decision of 16 June 2022 fined Rossel 50,000 euros for similar practices on three sites
issues.source_says: Not in this decision; Rossel appears only in the list of the 20 sites examined.

proposed_takeaway: In its first thematic investigation the Belgian DPA's Inspection Service examined the 20 most visited Belgian news sites for cookie use, consent and transparency, and fined Roularta 50,000 euros for cookies placed before consent, statistics cookies treated as exempt from consent, pre-ticked partner choices, a disclaimer for third-party cookies, deficient information, excessive cookie lifetimes and ineffective withdrawal on two of its sites, with an order to comply within three months. A parallel decision of 16 June 2022 fined Rossel 50,000 euros for similar practices on three sites. Publishers in Belgium should expect sector-wide sweeps with technical evidence and orders addressed to each violation.
note: Decision 85/2022 of 25 May 2022, 50,000 euro fine, two sites (knack.be, levif.be), 20 most visited sites and three-month compliance order confirmed.

file_used: Guidance note on cookies and other tracking technologies.txt

issues.claim: It remains the operative Irish standard for banner design
issues.source_says: Not addressed by the document (Version last updated April 2020).

note: Regulation 5(3) S.I. 336/2011 (p. 2), Planet49 and pre-checked boxes/sliders (pp. 8, 10), equal prominence for reject (p. 9) and withdrawal as easy as giving (p. 11), analytics need consent with first-party analytics unlikely to be an enforcement priority (pp. 7-8), six-month reaffirmation (pp. 8, 11), shopping-basket session cookies exempt (p. 8) all confirmed.

note: Report dated 6 April 2020, sweep August to December 2019, sectors listed (p. 2), adtech core to business models (p. 2), widespread bad practice (p. 8), published with new guidance and a six-month compliance window (p. 8) all confirmed. The document's own title page reads 'Report dated: 6 April 2020' although the file name says revised 15 April 2020.

issues.claim: could not prevent access under FISA 702 and EO 12333
issues.source_says: Operative point 2(b): Google LLC is an electronic communications service provider under 50 USC 1881(b)(4) and subject to surveillance under 50 USC 1881a (FISA 702); the supplementary measures do not eliminate that access. EO 12333 appears only in the summary of Schrems II and in the parties' submissions, not in the findings.

issues.claim: date 13 January 2022 (entry date)
issues.source_says: The decision (German original, last page) is dated 22 December 2021, electronically signed 12 January 2022; 13 January 2022 is the noyb publication date.

issues.claim: the first decision on noyb's 101 complaints; adopted by other authorities in 2022; EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted in July 2023
issues.source_says: Not in the document (it refers to the case as '101 Dalmatians' but does not say it is the first decision).

proposed_takeaway: In the first decision on noyb's 101 complaints after Schrems II, the DSB held that an Austrian website's use of Google Analytics transferred personal data (identifiers, IP address, browser data) to the United States in breach of Chapter V GDPR, because the standard contractual clauses and Google's supplementary measures could not prevent access by US intelligence services under FISA 702. The reasoning was adopted by other authorities in 2022 and drove the move to consent-gated or EU-hosted analytics. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted in July 2023 changed the transfer basis, but the analysis of what analytics tags actually send remains the practical checklist.
note: Partial decision (Teilbescheid): complaint upheld against the website operator, rejected against Google LLC. Decision date 22 December 2021; consider correcting the entry date. Machine translation used; cross-checked with the German original.

issues.claim: three cookie banner decisions, 30 April 2025 (title and entry date)
issues.source_says: The decisions are dated 4 October 2024 (Warner Music, IMY-2023-16448), 16 December 2024 (ATG, IMY-2023-16453) and 28 April 2025 (Aller Media, IMY-2023-16452); 30 April 2025 is the IMY news item.

issues.claim: ATG for misleading banner design that hindered informed and voluntary consent
issues.source_says: ATG decision p. 1: breach of Arts 6 and 7(3) both for not making withdrawal as easy as giving consent and for misleading banner design that hindered informed and voluntary consent.

issues.claim: Investigating complaints from individuals abroad
issues.source_says: Each decision says the complaint is one of several lodged with European data protection authorities and handled through the EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce, with Austria, Italy (and Denmark for Aller) as concerned authorities; the complainants' residence is not stated.

proposed_takeaway: Investigating complaints channelled through the EDPB cookie banner taskforce, IMY reprimanded Warner Music Sweden (October 2024) for not adequately informing users of the right to withdraw consent (articles 6 and 7(3) GDPR), ATG (December 2024) for not making withdrawal as easy as consent and for misleading banner design that hindered informed and voluntary consent, and Aller Media (April 2025) for processing without a legal basis by citing legitimate interest for cookie data without a documented balancing test (article 6(1)(f)). IMY noted that the Post and Telecom Authority (PTS) alone supervises the Electronic Communications Act's cookie rules, while IMY supervises the subsequent GDPR processing. Swedish-facing sites need a documented basis for post-consent processing, not only a banner.
note: Also relied on tillsynsbeslut-aktiebolaget-trav-och-galopp.txt and tillsynsbeslut-aller-media-ab.txt. Reprimands under Art. 58(2)(b), PTS competence statement and the Aller legitimate-interest reasoning (pp. 4-5) confirmed.

issues.claim: Only cookies necessary for a requested service (login, security, payment) are exempt
issues.source_says: Section 3.2 (pp. 4-5): exempt cookies are those whose sole purpose is to carry out the transmission of a communication, or that are necessary to provide a service the user has explicitly requested. Worked examples in 3.3 are session login/authentication cookies, preference cookies (language, layout), user-input cookies (shopping basket, forms) and load balancing. 'Security' and 'payment' are not the guide's examples.

issues.claim: Helsinki Administrative Court rulings that transferred cookie consent questions to Traficom
issues.source_says: Page 2: the court's two rulings of 8 April 2021 (H1515/2021 and H1516/2021) held that browser settings cannot give valid consent and that Traficom is the competent authority for cookie regulation and supervision, including interpretation of consent for cookie purposes. 'Confirmed' rather than 'transferred'.

issues.claim: enforcement decisions against major Finnish providers for misclassifying cookies as necessary
issues.source_says: The decisions attached to the page (Telia 21.11.2023, Sanoma 8.6.2023, Nordea 16.12.2022, Posti 20.4.2022 and others) find breaches of section 205(1) for setting consent-requiring cookies without valid consent: consent by continued browsing (Nordea), cookies set despite user choices and an unclassified category (Telia), accept easier than reject (Telia). Misclassification as necessary appears in some (Suomalainen Kirjakauppa, DigiFinland) but is not the common ground.

issues.claim: The page records updates through 23 April 2026
issues.source_says: Not in the guide, which is dated 1.9.2021 (TRAFICOM/295680/04.04.05.03/2021); the entry date of 13 September 2021 is also not the document date.

proposed_takeaway: Following Helsinki Administrative Court rulings of 8 April 2021 that confirmed Traficom as the competent authority for cookie consent questions, the agency's guidance under section 205 of the Act on Electronic Communications Services (917/2014) states that consent for non-essential cookies cannot be given through browser settings, continued use or pre-ticked toggles, must be as easy to refuse as to give and as easy to withdraw, and that legitimate interest is not a basis for storing on the terminal. Only cookies whose sole purpose is transmitting a communication or that are necessary for a service the user has requested (session login, shopping basket, language choice, load balancing) are exempt. The page records updates through 23 April 2026 and enforcement decisions against major Finnish providers for setting consent-requiring cookies without valid consent.
note: Two identical copies of the guide were supplied; the remaining files are the enforcement decisions the page links. Guide itself is dated 1 September 2021 and says it is not legally binding.

issues.source_says: Neither supplied file is the cookie guidance: etiske-retningslinjer-dt-8-mai-2024 is Datatilsynet's internal staff ethics code, and slik-bruker-datatilsynet-kunstig-intelligens-pa-nettsiden is a one-page note on how Datatilsynet uses AI on its website. issues.source_says: Page 25: cookie walls, defined as blocking access to a site without acceptance of cookies, are incompatible with the GDPR. 'All' is not stated.

issues.source_says: Not in the bulletin, which never mentions the telecommunications or electronic communications law or UKE. The article is in the 'New technologies' section and page 2 states that not all articles in the bulletin represent the authority's official position.

proposed_takeaway: The Polish supervisory authority's March 2025 bulletin states that consent to cookies must be voluntary, informed, unambiguous and preceded by an active user action, that pre-ticked boxes are invalid, that withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it, that cookie walls which block access to a site unless cookies are accepted are incompatible with the GDPR, and that clear pre-consent information on data, recipients and purposes is required; it relies on EDPB Guidelines 05/2020, the EDPB cookie banner task force report and the CJEU judgments in Planet49 (C-673/17) and Orange Romania (C-61/19). The bulletin applies the GDPR consent standard to banners directly and notes that not every article in it states the authority's official position.

issues.claim: Issued after an audit of popular Greek websites found widespread non-compliance
issues.source_says: Page 1: the Authority 'has found to a considerable degree a lack of compliance' by information society service providers with the ePrivacy and GDPR requirements on cookies. No audit or 'popular websites' is described.

issues.source_says: Point C.7 (p. 5): the use of buttons and fonts of the same size, emphasis and colour is 'recommended' (συνιστάται), not mandated like the other C points.

issues.claim: under Law 3471/2006
issues.source_says: The text refers only to 'the special legislation for electronic communications' and the GDPR; Law 3471/2006 is not cited by number.

issues.claim: The HDPA re-invoked points C4 and C7 in its 2022 action on news websites
issues.source_says: Not in this 2020 document.

proposed_takeaway: Issued after the authority found widespread non-compliance by Greek website operators, the recommendations under Law 3471/2006 require prior consent for every tracker not technically necessary, including third-party analytics such as Google Analytics, with a two-month grace period. Accepting and refusing must take the same number of clicks from the same layer, withdrawal must be as easy as consent, access may not be restricted for refusal, buttons and fonts should share size, emphasis and colour, and the storage period of a refusal must equal that of an acceptance. Scrolling, continued browsing, pre-ticked boxes and browser settings are invalid. The HDPA re-invoked points C4 and C7 in its 2022 action on news websites.
note: Points C.4 to C.8 and the two-month deadline are confirmed verbatim; the scope also covers fingerprinting, local storage and OS identifiers.

issues.claim: noyb states that the Swedish IMY has received at least 56 complaints against Schibsted since the Swedish rollout
issues.source_says: Not in the complaint. It says only that Schibsted introduced similar banners on its Swedish sites first (para. 11) and that 64 consumers contacted Forbrukerrådet between 28 April and 2 June 2026 (para. 9). IMY is not mentioned.

proposed_takeaway: noyb filed a complaint with Datatilsynet, in cooperation with the Norwegian Consumer Council, alleging that Schibsted's requirement that readers of vg.no either accept tracking for personalised advertising or pay 49 NOK a month produces consent rates near 99 percent although only about 3 percent of users want to be tracked, so consent is not freely given under Articles 5(1), 6(1) and 7 GDPR. The complaint records that 64 consumers contacted the Consumer Council about the model between 28 April and 2 June 2026 and that Schibsted rolled the model out on its Swedish sites first. The complaint is pending; Nordic publishers should expect the first consent-or-pay decisions on news sites under the GDPR to come from this case.

issues.claim: The guidelines set four criteria for Article 5(3)
issues.source_says: Executive summary and para. 6 (section 2.1): three criteria, A 'information', B 'terminal equipment of a subscriber or user' (B.1) which implies assessing 'public communications network' (B.2), and C 'storage' (C.1) or 'gaining of access' (C.2). The takeaway's four items are the sub-criteria, not the document's count.

issues.claim: find that each falls within Article 5(3) where the instruction to send information comes from code the entity distributed
issues.source_says: True for pixels/URLs (para. 51), local processing (53), IoT (60) and unique identifiers (63). For IP-only tracking paras 54-55 say Article 5(3) can apply even where the instruction came from a different entity, provided the IP address originates from the user's terminal equipment.

issues.claim: Treat server-side tagging, link decoration, fingerprinting and pixel calls as consent events unless an exemption applies
issues.source_says: Server-side tagging is not named; para. 56 recalls that applicability of Article 5(3) does not automatically mean consent is needed and that exemptions must be assessed case by case. Advice is consistent with the text.

proposed_takeaway: The guidelines set three criteria for Article 5(3): information, whether personal or not; terminal equipment of a user, which requires a connection to a public communications network; and storage of, or gaining access to, that information. Paragraphs 47 to 63 apply them to URL and pixel tracking, local processing whose output is sent to a third party, tracking based on IP address alone, IoT reporting and unique identifiers, and find that each falls within Article 5(3) where the instruction to send information comes from code the entity distributed or, for IP-only tracking, where the address originates from the user's terminal equipment. Treat server-side tagging, link decoration, fingerprinting and pixel calls as consent events unless an exemption applies. Version 1.0 of 14 November 2023 is superseded.
note: Version 2.0 adopted 7 October 2024 after public consultation; version 1.0 of 14 November 2023 was the consultation draft.

Para. 39 (cookie walls) and para. 86 (scrolling or swiping) confirmed; preface states references to WP259 rev.01 are now read as references to these guidelines. Text is version 1.1 of 13 May 2020 (formatting corrections to the 4 May 2020 adoption). Second file is a Ukrainian translation.

'One-stop-shop' is the takeaway's label for the cooperation mechanism.

issues.source_says: The Opinion is expressly scoped to 'large online platforms' as defined in section 2.1.3; it discusses publishers only once, in passing, as part of the general description of the behavioural-advertising ecosystem (para. 20), and never states that authorities extend its reasoning to publishers.

proposed_takeaway: The report records the positions supervisory authorities share on the noyb banner complaints: a first layer with an accept button but no reject option is non-compliant (paragraphs 6 to 8); pre-ticked boxes do not create consent (paragraphs 9 to 10); a reject option hidden as a small link or outside the banner is insufficient (paragraphs 11 to 14); unreadable button contrast is manifestly misleading (paragraph 18); legitimate interest cannot ground a cookie under Article 5(3) (paragraphs 20 to 25); operators must prove and keep updated the list of essential cookies (paragraph 28); and withdrawal must be as easy as consent (paragraph 34). It sets the common enforcement baseline.
note: All other paragraph citations check out against the text. On the type A practice, paragraph 8 itself records that a 'vast majority' of authorities (not all) reached that view; the takeaway's flat wording is a defensible compression of that common denominator, so not flagged as an error.

Joint-controllership scope (collection/transmission only, not the platform's later processing), the Wirtschaftsakademie/Fashion ID basis, and the Article 5(3)/legitimate-interest-excluded/Article 26 points all match the text (e.g. lines 580-663, 1311-1318). All four paragraph citations check out precisely: para. 23 (one-off purchase/Art 6(1)(b) necessity), para. 47 (Art 6(1)(c) necessity unlikely to be met), paras. 58-75 (order tracking, subsequent changes, loyalty, future purchases, fraud prevention all failing the Art 6(1)(f) necessity/balancing tests), and para. 89 (guest option as most efficient design). Consent-fatigue framing, the cross-instrument split creating legal uncertainty (lines 339-341), the Article 88a(4) six-month bar (para. 106) welcomed via the broader Article 88a(4) safeguards (para. 105, 'very much welcome'), the strong support for Article 88b machine-readable signals (para. 108, line 1965), the audience-measurement/contextual-advertising asks (paras. 101-104), and the serious objection to narrowing the definition of personal data and to implementing acts (paras. 14-24) all check out against the text.

It addressed the Commission, not operators. Practitioners meet it as one of the reasons the pledge is understood to have stalled and as an early statement of positions later formalised in Opinion 08/2024. Treat it as background only; the operative EDPB positions are in Opinion 08/2024 and the Cookie Banner Taskforce report.

issues.claim: personalised advertising ... is not necessary for the contract under Article 6(1)(b) and cannot be justified as a legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f)
issues.source_says: Operative points 4 and 5: the Court sets conditions rather than a prohibition. Article 6(1)(b) applies only where the processing is objectively indispensable to a purpose integral to the contract; Article 6(1)(f) only where users were informed of the interest, the processing is strictly necessary and the balancing does not favour the users.

proposed_takeaway: The Grand Chamber held that a competition authority may examine GDPR compliance when assessing abuse of dominance, provided it cooperates with the supervisory authorities; that collecting data from other group services and third-party sites is necessary for the contract under Article 6(1)(b) only where it is objectively indispensable to a purpose integral to the contract, and can rest on Article 6(1)(f) only where the interest was disclosed to users, the processing is strictly necessary and the balancing favours the controller; and that a dominant position does not by itself invalidate consent but is an important factor in judging whether it was freely given, with the burden on the operator. Visiting a website revealing sensitive characteristics does not make that data manifestly public. Treat contract and legitimate interest as hard to sustain for off-site tracking data used in ad personalisation.

issues.claim: A new Article 88b ... with a six-month grace period
issues.source_says: Article 88b(5): paragraphs 1 and 2 (honouring machine-readable consent/refusal signals) apply from 24 months after entry into force; Article 88b(7): paragraph 6 (browser providers) applies from 48 months after entry into force. The six-month period in the proposal belongs to Article 88a (its own application date, and the minimum wait before re-asking for consent after a refusal), not to Article 88b.

issues.claim: As of September 2026 the file remains in committee with no Council general approach and no trilogue.
issues.source_says: The supplied text is the Council document transmitting the Commission proposal dated 20 November 2025; it does not itself state the procedure's status as of September 2026.

proposed_takeaway: The proposal moves the rules on storing and accessing personal data on terminal equipment from Article 5(3) ePrivacy into a new GDPR Article 88a, which keeps consent as the default, exempts transmission, requested services, aggregated first-party audience measurement and security, and bars a fresh consent request for the same purpose for at least six months after a refusal. A new Article 88b obliges controllers to honour automated, machine-readable consent and refusal signals once standards exist, applying from 24 months after entry into force, and requires browser providers other than SMEs to offer the feature from 48 months after entry into force. As of September 2026 the file remains in committee with no Council general approach and no trilogue.
note: Everything else (88a mechanics, exemptions, six-month cooldown, browser mandate) matches the text; only the timing attached to Article 88b was wrong.

issues.claim: including foreign operators with a real and substantial connection to Canada
issues.source_says: The statutory text does not use this phrase; it is a jurisdictional test from case law applying PIPEDA extraterritorially, not stated in the Act itself.

issues.source_says: The consolidated Act text (current to 21 July 2026) does not mention Bill C-36 or any pending replacement bill.

All eight criteria (manifeste, libre, eclaire, specifique, granulaire, comprehensible, temporaire, distinct), the disproportionate-effort and visual-emphasis points, the genuine-opportunity-to-refuse requirement for implied consent, and the non-binding status of the guidelines all match the text.

Cookie classifications, the consent/legitimate-interest pairing (including legitimate interest being unsuitable for profiling and advertising), the first- and second-layer banner requirements, default-off non-necessary cookies, and the listed non-compliant practices all match the guide.

issues.claim: including for analytics or necessary cookies
issues.source_says: This guide never mentions cookies; it addresses legitimate interest generally under Article 7, IX and Article 10 LGPD. The cookie application is a reasonable extension but is not stated here.

note: The four balancing-test factors, the Article 7,IX/Article 10 basis, the annex model, the sensitive-data exclusion and the restricted public-sector use all match the text.

issues.claim: permits direct marketing to children only with consent, in the child's best interests and from information collected directly from the child
issues.source_says: Section 11(3) (non-sensitive information): direct marketing needs consent plus consistency with the child's best interests. Section 11(4) (sensitive information): direct marketing needs the information to have been collected from the child or a person with parental responsibility, an opt-out mechanism (s29), and consistency with best interests, but does not itself require consent. The takeaway merges elements of both subsections into one requirement that matches neither.

proposed_takeaway: The draft Code, released on 31 March 2026 for consultation to 5 June 2026, would apply to APP entities providing social media, relevant electronic services or designated internet services likely to be accessed by children, other than health services. It requires collection, use and disclosure to be consistent with the child's best interests, and limits direct marketing to children: non-sensitive information may be used only with consent and consistently with the child's best interests, while sensitive information may be used only if it was collected from the child or a person with parental responsibility, an opt-out mechanism is offered, and the use is consistent with the child's best interests. It also requires age-appropriate notices and a deletion right. The final Code must be registered by 10 December 2026. Inventory trackers on child-accessible services now and plan to disable advertising and profiling cookies for those audiences.
note: Registration deadline confirmed (Short Guide and Extended Guide both state the final Code must be ready by 10 December 2026); consultation window and 'likely to be accessed by children' trigger both confirmed against the Explanatory Statement.

issues.claim: require an opt-out from targeted online behavioural advertising with an ad-free alternative where a service relies on marketing revenue
issues.source_says: The consultation paper's direct marketing section (p.19-20) says the framework 'retains the requirement for a simple opt-out mechanism' and 'provides flexibility for ad-supported services', and states plainly that 'the framework does not require consent for direct marketing'. Online behavioural advertising is covered by the ordinary direct-marketing opt-out. Neither the exposure draft bill nor the consultation paper contains any 'ad-free alternative' requirement; the paper's language points the other way, preserving ad-supported models.

issues.claim: confirm that IP addresses, device identifiers and cookie IDs are personal information where reasonably linkable
issues.source_says: The bill's Note 1 to the 'reasonably identifiable' definition (line ~605) lists examples: name, date of birth, address, contact information, a pseudonym or identifier, location/geolocation data, and behavioural characteristics or patterns of activity. Neither 'IP address', 'device identifier' nor 'cookie ID' appears anywhere in the bill or the consultation paper; the takeaway names specific technical identifiers the document itself does not name.

proposed_takeaway: The Attorney-General's Department released the tranche 2 exposure draft, with the Bill and an accompanying consultation paper, in 2026. It would define consent as voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous, extend collection to information generated or inferred, give identifiers and location or behavioural data as examples of information that is personal where reasonably linkable, make precise geolocation tracking data sensitive, add a fair and reasonable test weighing the child's best interests, require consent before trading personal information, and retain a simple opt-out from direct marketing, including online behavioural advertising based on personal information, while keeping flexibility for ad-supported services. It is not law. Model banner changes now against the proposed standard.
note: Could not confirm the 31 August 2026 release date or 18 September 2026 consultation closing date from the text of either file; no dates of that kind appear in the extracted text, so this was left unverified rather than flagged as wrong.

Article 31(1) and its cross-referenced confirmation/recording mechanics (via Article 30) match the takeaway; Article 171 confirms extraterritorial application to foreign businesses serving people in Japan. The official translation renders the Article 2(7) term as 'information related to personal information' rather than 'personally referable information', but this is a translation-label difference, not a substantive discrepancy.

Guidelines cover page confirms first issue November 2016 (Heisei 28) and partial revision June 2026 (Reiwa 8), matching the amendment comparison table in the second file. Section 2-8 (line 1304) defines personally referable information and gives Cookie-based device identifiers and browsing history as an explicit example; the Article 31 third-party provision/confirmation rules sit in section 3-7, which the takeaway's guidance to 'use section 2-8' does not misstate since 2-8 is what is needed to classify a tag before applying the 3-7 confirmation duty.

Cover page confirms first issued 16 Feb 2017, updated 1 July 2025. The second file (tsuikakoushin) is an unrelated update about safeguards against unauthorised computer access, not about cookies or Article 31, but it was not relied on for this takeaway's claims.

Assent date (11 August 2023), section 6 consent elements, Consent Manager, section 9 parental consent/tracking-and-advertising prohibition for under-18s, and the Schedule penalties (250 crore for section 8(5) security failures, 200 crore for section 9 children's obligations) all match exactly.

Sections 11, 18, 69 and 109 match the takeaway's description exactly, including the R10 million administrative fine cap. Commencement/grace-period dates (1 July 2020 / 30 June 2021) are not stated in the Act's own text (they were fixed by separate proclamation) but are not contradicted by anything in the document.

Publication date (20 March 2025), commencement the day after publication (21 March 2025), repeal of the 5 July 2010 statute, the Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno as new supervisor, tacit/express consent rules (articles 7-8), and the transfer exceptions (articles 9 and 36, including group companies and contracts in the person's interest) all match. The cookie/web-beacon disclosure duty is correctly attributed to separate implementing regulations rather than to this Law, which this file does not include, so it could not be checked directly.

TC Strings created before the deadline remain valid until users refresh their choices. The change binds TCF-registered CMPs and vendors by contract, not law; confirm that your CMP's TC Strings carry the segment and that each vendor's ID bit is set.

proposed_takeaway: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment against a plaintiff who alleged that Salesforce's chat software on a retailer's website violated CIPA section 631(a), finding no evidence from which a jury could conclude that Salesforce made an unauthorised connection with a telephone wire or read messages in transit. A concurrence went further and reasoned that the section's reference to telegraph or telephone wires does not reach internet communications. The unpublished memorandum applies to operators deploying third-party chat and similar vendors. Keep evidence of what the vendor's software actually accesses or reads, since the plaintiff's inability to show that Salesforce read her messages, rather than merely being capable of doing so, was fatal to the claim.

proposed_takeaway: Supervisory authorities applying the Article 6(1)(f) three-step test in 67 decisions between December 2018 and June 2025 (62 one-stop-shop decisions and 5 EDPB binding decisions) accepted commercial interests only when stated precisely, frequently failed controllers at the necessity stage where a less intrusive design existed, and read data subjects' interests and reasonable expectations broadly. The common infringements were no documented assessment before processing began, vague interests such as measuring content performance, retroactive reliance on legitimate interest to keep data collected without a legal basis, and transparency gaps that stopped people objecting. Controllers relying on legitimate interest should write the assessment first, name the interest specifically and disclose it. proposed_takeaway: Across 32 supervisory authorities and 764 controllers surveyed, erasure compliance is mostly rated average and fails in seven recurring ways: missing internal procedures (flagged by 17 authorities), untrained staff, thin privacy notice information (13 authorities), blanket use of Article 17(3) exceptions without documented case-by-case assessment, retention periods that controllers struggle to define per purpose (one applied the longest period to everything), no method for erasure in back-ups, and anonymisation used as a substitute for deletion. Nine authorities opened or continued formal investigations. Controllers should adopt a written erasure procedure with owners and deadlines, a data deletion matrix cross-referencing data types and retention periods, a back-up erasure method, and documented reasoning for every refusal.

issues.claim: ask for recitals confirming ... that the threshold follows the formal SME and SMC definitions
issues.source_says: Para. 28 (p. 11-12) recommends that the amended Article 30(5) GDPR itself refer to the newly introduced SME and SMC definitions in place of 'enterprise'; that is a change to the enacting text, not a recital. The other three requests (records only for high-risk activities, Article 9(2)(b), public authorities) are indeed recital clarifications (executive summary p. 3-4, paras 17 and 32).

proposed_takeaway: The Commission's proposal of 21 May 2025 would raise the Article 30(5) record-keeping exemption from fewer than 250 employees to fewer than 750, drop the trigger for special category and criminal data, and keep records only for processing likely to result in high risk, covering an estimated 38,000 SMCs. The EDPB and EDPS accept the aim, note the missing fundamental rights assessment and ask for clarifications: recitals confirming that records are needed only for the high-risk activities themselves, that Article 9(2)(b) employment processing is in principle not high risk and that public authorities stay excluded, and a reference in Article 30(5) itself to the formal SME and SMC definitions. Until adoption, the 250-employee rule applies.
note: Adopted 8 July 2025 (packet date 9 July is publication). 21 May 2025, 750, 38,000 SMCs (para. 24 and fn 46), missing fundamental rights assessment, Article 9/10 trigger deletion (para. 15) and Article 9(2)(b) recital (para. 17) all confirmed.

issues.claim: in practice is usually a narrowly read Article 49 derogation, since a foreign authority rarely signs Article 46 safeguards
issues.source_says: Para. 37 (p. 12) says Article 49 derogations 'must be interpreted restrictively' and apply in 'a limited number of specific situations'; footnote 18 (p. 11) says the EDPB 'is not aware of the existence of many international agreements' providing Article 46(2)(a) safeguards. The document does not say Article 49 is 'usually' the ground in practice; that is the takeaway's inference.

proposed_takeaway: A request from a third-country court or authority is not in itself a legal basis for processing nor a ground for transfer: the controller or processor needs an Article 6 basis and a Chapter V transfer tool. A mutual legal assistance treaty or similar agreement can supply both, as a legal obligation or public interest task under Article 6(1)(c) or (e) and as appropriate safeguards under Article 46(2)(a); without one, the organisation still needs an Article 6 basis and a Chapter V ground, which in practice is usually a narrowly read Article 49 derogation, since few international agreements of this kind exist. Processors receiving such requests must inform the controller promptly. Version 2.0 was adopted 4 June 2025 after consultation on the December 2024 draft; version 2.1 of 20 June 2025 only improves the resolution of the annex.
note: Version 1.0 adopted 2 December 2024 for consultation, 2.0 on 4 June 2025; processor duty to inform controller without undue delay confirmed at para. 18 and the annex.

issues.claim: five-module ... terminology and the AI lifecycle, GDPR principles and AI Act risk tiers mapped onto AI risks, secure MLOps and secure processing environments, deployment, monitoring and decommissioning, and audit checklists
issues.source_says: Book structure (p. 7): module 1 covers basic terminology and the lifecycle (chapters 1 to 3, which include the GDPR principles, AI Act risk tiers and the AI/privacy risk mapping; chapter 3.4 says 'we conclude this introductory module'); module 2 covers 'the data privacy aspects of the AI systems life-cycle: data collection, privacy enhancing technologies, and in general all the (personal) data flows before putting the system in production'; module 3 development, secure sandboxes and testing; module 4 deployment, monitoring, sustainability and decommissioning; module 5 audit checklists and use cases. The takeaway's second item describes module 1 content and the data management and PETs module is missing.

proposed_takeaway: Security, data science and governance teams running AI systems on personal data get shared vocabulary and lifecycle controls from this five-module open-source training (CC BY-SA 4.0): terminology, the AI lifecycle and GDPR principles and AI Act risk tiers mapped onto AI risks; personal data management and privacy-enhancing technologies before production; secure MLOps, testing and secure processing environments; deployment, monitoring and decommissioning; and audit checklists with worked use cases. It maps seven AI risk domains against the ten privacy risks in ISO/IEC 29134:2023. An external SPE expert wrote it, submitted December 2024 and updated April 2025, and it carries no official EDPB position. Use it as a curriculum and a source of AI/ML audit questions.
note: CC-BY-SA 4.0 (p. 6), 'submitted in December 2024, updated in April 2025' (p. 5), seven AI risk domains from Slattery et al. (p. 30) and ten ISO/IEC 29134:2023 privacy risks (p. 31-32) all confirmed; commissioned by the EDPB and the Greek DPA under the SPE programme.

issues.claim: Expect data-sharing and default-setting practices of dominant firms to be reviewed by both regulators.
issues.source_says: The paper discusses combination and cross-use of personal data by gatekeepers (para 10, DMA Article 5(2)), the validity of consent where a dominant position creates an imbalance (paras 11 and 12) and competition authorities assessing general terms of use on personal data processing (para 13). It does not mention default settings.

proposed_takeaway: Data protection and competition law pursue distinct objectives but both protect the individual, as data subject and as consumer, and personal data is central to digital business models, so the two sets of authorities must coordinate. Following the CJEU judgment in Meta v Bundeskartellamt, a competition authority assessing abuse of dominance may need to examine GDPR compliance but cannot replace the competent data protection authority, and the principle of sincere cooperation makes cooperation mandatory in some cases. The paper recommends dedicated coordination teams, cooperation protocols with deadlines and information-sharing rules, and joint sector inquiries. Expect the data combination, terms of use and consent practices of dominant firms to be reviewed by both regulators.
note: Everything else confirmed: sincere cooperation and 'cannot replace' at para 13, dedicated team at para 24, protocols at para 25, deadlines and information sharing at para 22, joint sector inquiries at para 26.

issues.claim: Processors must flow identical obligations down to sub-processors
issues.source_says: Para 63 (page 17): sub-processing contracts must impose 'the same data protection obligations' along the chain, but 'it is not required that the sub-processing contract is identical in wording' to the initial contract.

proposed_takeaway: Controllers must have the name, address and contact person of every processor and sub-processor in the chain readily available at all times, and must verify that each provides sufficient guarantees, with the extent of verification scaling with the risk of the processing. Processors must flow the same data protection obligations down to sub-processors, though the contract wording need not be identical, and the controller need not systematically review sub-processing contracts; it decides case by case whether doing so is needed for accountability. The controller remains responsible for transfers made by processors and sub-processors and needs the transfer mapping and legal grounds documented. Requested by the Danish supervisory authority; use it to rebuild sub-processor inventories and due diligence.
note: Danish SA request, identity information readily available at all times, risk-scaled verification, no systematic contract review and transfer mapping (para 100 onwards) all confirmed. Adopted 7 October 2024; the 9 October page date is not in the takeaway.

They express the external author's views and not an EDPB position, and are aimed at supervisory authorities inspecting AI systems as well as those developing and acquiring them, with reference to the AI Act. Use the checklist as a starting structure for internal AI audits, the leaflet format for transparency towards buyers and implementors, and the algo-score idea for end-user facing labels.

issues.claim: two reports prepared for the EDPS under the Support Pool of Experts programme
issues.source_says: Neither report mentions the EDPS; both carry the standard note that the EDPB commissions SPE deliverables (p. 2). The EDPS attribution cannot be checked from the text.

issues.claim: written both for controllers assessing risk and for authorities checking the validity of those assessments during investigations
issues.source_says: The reports address risks and mitigations from the perspective of the 'user, procurement entity and developer' (OCR pp. 12, 40 ff.; NER same structure); they do not describe a role for authorities checking assessments during investigations. The only 'investigations' mentioned are criminal investigations as an example of harm (NER p. 21).

proposed_takeaway: Optical character recognition and named entity recognition carry specific data protection risks across procurement, development and use, and two reports prepared under the Support Pool of Experts programme list those risks with possible mitigations for each phase. They are the external author's views, not an EDPB position, and are written for the users, developers and procuring entities of such systems, with criteria for assessing likelihood and severity and for accepting residual risk. Use the risk catalogues when running a DPIA on document digitisation, redaction or entity extraction pipelines.
note: Both reports by Isabel Barbera, submitted September 2023, technology state of the art as of August 2023. Verify the EDPS attribution against the EDPB web page before dropping it.

issues.claim: Central databases under airport operator control and cloud storage under airline control cannot satisfy data protection by design and breach the security and storage limitation requirements.
issues.source_says: Executive summary pp. 3 to 4: both scenarios cannot be compatible with Article 25 and would not comply with Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 if the controller limited itself to the described measures. Non-compliance with storage limitation (Article 5(1)(e)) is found only for the cloud scenario (scenario 4); the airport database scenario (scenario 3) has a typical 48 hour retention and no storage limitation finding.

proposed_takeaway: Facial recognition to speed passengers through airport checkpoints is compatible with Articles 5(1)(e), 5(1)(f), 25 and 32 GDPR only where the biometric template stays under the passenger's control: stored solely on the passenger's device, or stored centrally at the airport encrypted with a key held only by the passenger. Central databases under airport operator control and cloud storage under airline control cannot satisfy data protection by design and would not meet the security requirements with the measures described, and the cloud scenario also fails storage limitation. Requested by the French supervisory authority and adopted 23 May 2024, it guides airport operators, airlines and their authorities; any biometric passenger flow project must be built around on-device storage or passenger-held keys.
note: Version 1.1 of 28 May 2024 only corrected grammar; adoption date 23 May 2024 and FR SA request (16 February 2024) confirmed.
