issues.claim: starting with the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence's Civil Liberties Protection Officer
issues.source_says: Complaints have to be sent to the national EU/EEA DPA, which verifies identity and completeness and transmits the complaint, encrypted, to the EDPB Secretariat, which forwards it to the ODNI CLPO (pages 2 to 4). The CLPO is the first US reviewer, not the starting point for the individual.

issues.claim: can complain through the Data Privacy Framework redress mechanism
issues.source_says: The mechanism was established by E.O. 14086 and applies regardless of the transfer tool used (DPF, SCCs, BCRs, codes, certification, derogations), but only to data transmitted after 10 July 2023 (page 2).

issues.claim: rules of procedure for the mechanism and for the informal panel of EU data protection authorities that handles them
issues.source_says: The note only says the EDPB has adopted Rules of Procedure to guide DPAs (page 3); it does not mention an informal panel.

issues.claim: Controllers relying on the DPF should reference the mechanism in their transfer documentation and privacy notices
issues.source_says: Not addressed in the note, which is written for complainants and DPAs.

proposed_takeaway: Individuals in the EU and EEA who believe their personal data transferred to the United States was unlawfully collected or processed by US national security authorities can complain through the redress mechanism created by Executive Order 14086, whatever transfer tool was used, for data transmitted after 10 July 2023: the complaint goes to their national data protection authority, which checks it and passes it via the EDPB Secretariat to the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence's Civil Liberties Protection Officer, with a right of appeal to the Data Protection Review Court within 60 days. Complaints use the EDPB template complaint form for the CLPO, and the note sits alongside rules of procedure for the mechanism and for the informal panel of EU data protection authorities that handles them. Controllers transferring data to the US under any tool should reference the mechanism in their transfer documentation and privacy notices.
note: The note itself carries no adoption date in the text; the 60-day DPRC appeal window and the DPA-first routing are the substantive points the original blurs.

issues.claim: platforms should offer a further free alternative without behavioural advertising
issues.source_says: Executive summary and paragraphs 74 to 76: controllers 'should consider also offering' a further alternative free of charge; 'there is no obligation for large online platforms to always offer services free of charge', but doing so makes freely given consent easier to demonstrate.

issues.claim: with a corrigendum in October 2024
issues.source_says: The corrigendum file lists editorial corrections (paragraphs 49 and 60, several footnotes) but carries no date; the October 2024 date cannot be checked from the documents.

proposed_takeaway: Large online platforms that offer users only a choice between consenting to behavioural advertising or paying a fee will, in most cases, not obtain valid consent. Consent must be freely given, so platforms should consider offering a further free alternative without behavioural advertising, for instance contextual advertising using less or no personal data, and must assess detriment, lock-in effects, the power imbalance flowing from market position and whether any fee is appropriate at all; the controller bears the burden of demonstrating all of this. Requested by the Dutch, Norwegian and Hamburg authorities and adopted 17 April 2024, with an editorial corrigendum in October 2024, it addresses large online platforms only.
note: Requesting authorities, adoption date, scope limitation and accountability burden all confirmed.

issues.claim: a breach occurring does not by itself prove that security measures were inappropriate
issues.source_says: Section 3, page 8: the digest takes this from Advocate General Pitruzzella's opinion in C-340/21 (judgment then pending), not from the SA decisions themselves; the AG said the mere existence of a breach is not in itself sufficient to conclude measures were not appropriate.

issues.claim: must be notified separately with enough detail for the authority to verify compliance
issues.source_says: Section 4.1, pages 25 to 26: two distinct findings. (1) In EDPBI:IE:OSS:D:2020:165 the breach documentation under Article 33(5) was too general to let the LSA verify compliance with Article 33. (2) In EDPBI:NL:OSS:D:2020:173 the controller had to notify each breach after it occurs even if it considered it linked to others. The takeaway merges the documentation point into the notification.

issues.claim: Prepared by an external expert under the Support Pool of Experts programme
issues.source_says: Not stated in the text (the cover page is blank in the conversion); the document only calls itself a 'Thematic Document'. The claim comes from the EDPB web page classification.

proposed_takeaway: Ninety final one-stop-shop decisions adopted between January 2019 and June 2023 show how supervisory authorities apply Articles 32, 33 and 34: a breach occurring does not by itself prove that security measures were inappropriate (a point the digest draws from the Advocate General's opinion in C-340/21), and authorities assess encryption, access controls, password policies and logging case by case across external attacks, weak internal practices and human error. Each notifiable breach (Article 33(1): any breach unless it is unlikely to result in a risk) must be notified separately even if the controller thinks it linked to others, breach documentation under Article 33(5) must be detailed enough for the authority to verify compliance, and the risk assessment decides whether affected individuals must be informed. Prepared by an external expert under the Support Pool of Experts programme; use it to calibrate breach severity and notification decisions against decided cases.
note: Count of 90 decisions, date range and register consultation window (10 July to 31 August 2023) confirmed on page 5.

issues.claim: most DPOs report the skills, training, clearly defined tasks and independence
issues.source_says: Supported by the medians (90.91% expert knowledge, 85.57% with a written task description, only 13.82% receiving instructions), but the report itself frames the picture as mixed: four SAs judged awareness and compliance low, ten judged it overall positive, and 'most respondents do not assign all of the required responsibilities to their DPOs' (pages 19, 30).

note: 25 SAs, 2023, second CEF, 17,490 completed questionnaires (page 9), all confirmed. Report is dated 'Adopted on 16 January 2024' on its cover; the packet date of 17 January 2024 is the publication date.

issues.claim: consent is the basis to design for
issues.source_says: Paragraph 151 to 152 and page 42: Meta's consent proposal 'was not assessed in its merits for the purposes of this urgent binding decision'; the EDPB only notes that the IE SA and CSAs are evaluating it. The decision does not endorse consent as the way forward.

issues.claim: For any controller, neither contract nor legitimate interest carries behavioural advertising
issues.source_says: The findings (paragraphs 152 to 153, 323) concern Meta IE's processing on Meta's products only; the generalisation is the takeaway's own reading.

proposed_takeaway: Meta Platforms Ireland infringed Article 6(1) GDPR by continuing to process personal data for behavioural advertising on Facebook and Instagram under Article 6(1)(b) after the Irish SA's decisions of 31 December 2022, and by switching to Article 6(1)(f) on 5 April 2023 without a valid legal basis. The EDPB instructed the Irish SA to order Meta to cease that processing across the entire EEA, extending the Norwegian SA's provisional ban of 14 July 2023; Meta's consent proposal was not assessed. For any controller the lesson is that neither contract nor legitimate interest carries behavioural advertising built on observed behaviour, location and ad interactions, which leaves consent as the basis to design for.
note: All dates, the Article 6(1)(b) and 6(1)(f) findings, the EEA-wide scope (paragraphs 309 to 310, 323) and the instruction to the IE SA (paragraph 324) are confirmed.

10 July 2023 application, no Article 46 tools or supplementary measures for DPF List recipients, Article 46 safeguards otherwise, Commission assessment to be taken into account, complaint without proof of collection, and the one-year then at-least-four-year review cycle are all in the note.

issues.claim: a referential of mandatory elements
issues.source_says: The document calls Chapter 3 'Elements and principles to be found in BCR-C' and never uses the word 'referential' (a WP256 term); the table asks applicants to insert references to the BCR sections addressing each requirement (page 19, footnote 14), which supports the 'map each element' instruction.

note: Replacement of WP256 rev.01 and WP264 (paragraphs 2 to 3), application to all BCR-C holders via the 2024 annual update generally without new approval (paragraph 15), single copy to the presumptive BCR Lead (page 7) and the Part I and Part II contents are all confirmed. Version 2.1 dated 20 June 2023 with an editorial correction of 3 July 2023.

issues.claim: apply to controllers and processors that are undertakings
issues.source_says: Paragraphs 9 to 10: the guidance applies to all controllers and processors except natural persons not acting as undertakings, and, where national law allows fines on public bodies, to public authorities too (with Chapters 4.3 and 6 excluded in some cases). The takeaway's wording is a fair simplification.

note: Five steps, the 0 to 10, 10 to 20 and 20 to 100 percent starting ranges (paragraphs 60 onward), turnover adjustment, aggravating and mitigating circumstances including cooperation and remedial action, legal maximum and the effectiveness, proportionality and dissuasiveness check are all confirmed. Version 2.1, adopted 24 May 2023, minor correction 29 June 2023.

issues.claim: encryption fails where the importer holds the keys
issues.source_says: Para 8, p. 5: encryption by the importer is not suitable where the importer, as tool provider, has legal obligations to provide the cryptographic keys. Close paraphrase.

issues.claim: Since 10 July 2023 the EU-US adequacy decision covers transfers to DPF-certified recipients
issues.source_says: Not in the report (dated 28 March 2023); the disclaimer on p. 3 only notes the positions may change if the legal framework changes.

note: Report dated 28 March 2023. Footnote 14 lists AT, DK, EE, ES, FI, FR, HU, IT (eight SAs) plus an EDPS decision. Disclaimer says the positions are those of the participating SAs, not the EDPB, which the takeaway reflects.

issues.claim: the EDPB ran a coordinated enforcement action on the right of access in 2024, reported in January 2025
issues.source_says: Not in the guidelines.

note: File is version 2.1 (30 May 2024, minor corrections) of the guidelines adopted 28 March 2023. Three components, free first copy, commonly used electronic form for electronic requests (para 32), one month plus two, layers all available at once if the data subject chooses (paras 146 to 147), narrow reading and burden of proof for Art. 12(5), and Art. 15(4) not applying to the Art. 15(1)(a) to (h) information (para 169) all match.

issues.claim: Version 2.1 adds that main establishment attaches to a single controller and cannot be extended to joint controllers
issues.source_says: Version history, p. 2, and preface paras 2 and 3: the joint controller clarification (section 2.1.3, para 35) is the substance of the 2022/2023 update adopted as version 2.0 on 28 March 2023. Version 2.1 (28 September 2023) only corrects footnote 12 on p. 10.

proposed_takeaway: The lead supervisory authority for cross-border processing is the authority of the main establishment: for a controller the place of central administration in the Union unless decisions on purposes and means are taken and implemented elsewhere, for a processor its central administration or, failing that, where the main processing takes place. The 2023 update adds that main establishment attaches to a single controller and cannot be extended to joint controllers, each of which keeps its own; version 2.1 only corrects a footnote. Forum shopping is not permitted, and a processor working for a controller established in the EEA is supervised by the controller's lead authority. The guidelines replace WP244 rev.01; document the main establishment analysis with objective evidence.
note: Para 41 limits the controller-lead rule for processors to controllers established in the EEA; added for precision.

Adopted 13 April 2023. Inquiry IN-20-8-1 commenced 28 August 2020 (para 2). Binding decision paras 272 to 279: fine for the Article 46(1) infringement and an order to bring processing into compliance with Chapter V by ceasing unlawful processing, including storage in the US, within six months. Addressed to the IE SA and the CSAs (para 280).

Version 2.0 adopted 28 March 2023. Preface paras 1 and 2: replaces WP250 rev.01, only para 73 (section II.C.2) revised. Para 73: representative does not trigger the one-stop-shop, so the breach is notified to every SA whose Member State has affected data subjects.

issues.claim: oversight and redress for security-related access remain underdeveloped
issues.source_says: Conclusion, p. 37, and executive summary, p. 4: what is missing is comprehensive data protection law for national security, public security, defence and criminal prosecution; national security and defence have less rigid legal limits, with the judiciary and legislature as the main oversight bodies. Section 2.2.2, p. 27 states that the legal framework provides for effective oversight of intelligence activities, and section 2.3.2 describes judicial redress and habeas data for everyone regardless of nationality. The study faults the substantive rules more than the oversight and redress machinery.

proposed_takeaway: Brazil's 2018 General Data Protection Law mirrors the GDPR and its authority ANPD became independent by 2022, but national security, public security, defence and criminal prosecution fall outside that law, judicial orders are required under the Civil Rights Framework for the Internet, and comprehensive data protection rules for security-related access are still lacking, with the judiciary and legislature as the main oversight bodies. The externally authored study, prepared for the EDPB, does not bind the EDPB or its members and is not an adequacy finding. Exporters can cite it in transfer impact assessments for Brazil as an evidence base on the law and practice of government access, alongside their own analysis.
note: ANPD became a special nature autarchy under Law 14.460/2022 (p. 20). Disclaimer on p. 2 supports the non-binding and non-adequacy statements. Study is dated April 2023.

issues.claim: a 2017 public-sector data protection law
issues.source_says: The body (p. 16, and the transparency section) dates the LGPDSSO to 2017, while the executive summary on p. 4 says 2015. The study is internally inconsistent; 2017 matches the body of the report.

note: Executive summary and conclusion (pp. 4, 62) confirm the ARCO rights for all persons, the 2005 National Security Law with fewer data protection provisions, expert reports of government attempts to diminish or discontinue the INAI (p. 24), the Turkish exemption of judicial, law enforcement and intelligence bodies, and the four Turkish concerns. Section 1.2 applies the Article 52(1) Charter test. Disclaimer p. 2: views do not reflect the EDPB's official opinion.

issues.claim: temporary bulk collection without prior independent authorisation
issues.source_says: Executive summary p. 5 and paras 144, 157 to 163: the lack of prior independent authorisation is raised for bulk collection under EO 12333 generally (para 163 says bulk collection is still provided without key safeguards such as prior authorisation), while temporary bulk collection is a separate point needing clarification. The takeaway compresses two related concerns into one clause.

issues.claim: The Commission adopted the adequacy decision on 10 July 2023
issues.source_says: Not in the opinion (adopted 28 February 2023).

note: Executive summary pp. 4 to 6 confirm necessity and proportionality, the EO binding the entire Intelligence Community (para 121), the DPRC, onward transfers, the DPRC standard non-appealable response, the need for specific automated decision-making rules, the recommendation to make adoption and entry into force conditional on updated agency policies and procedures, and the call to closely monitor the redress mechanism.

issues.claim: They address social media providers, designers and DPOs
issues.source_says: Executive summary (p. 3): the Guidelines offer recommendations to social media providers as controllers, designers and users of social media platforms; DPOs are named only as members of the interdisciplinary teams the EDPB recommends controllers use.

issues.claim: transparency in Article 12
issues.source_says: p. 4: transparency is listed as a principle under Article 5(1)(a); Article 12 is cited separately as a specific obligation on which the assessment is also based. Acceptable shorthand.

issues.claim: the EDPB applied the same reasoning in Binding Decision 2/2023
issues.source_says: Not in the document (adopted 14 February 2023, before that decision).

proposed_takeaway: Interfaces that push users into unintended or harmful choices about their data breach the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a), transparency in Article 12, data minimisation in Article 5(1)(c) and data protection by design in Article 25. The guidelines sort such patterns into six categories, overloading, skipping, stirring, obstructing, fickle and left in the dark, across registration, privacy notices, consent and settings, rights requests and account closure. They address social media providers, designers and users, recommend interdisciplinary teams that include DPOs, and version 2.0 renames dark patterns as deceptive design patterns. Use the categories as a review checklist for any consent or settings interface, since the EDPB applied the same reasoning in Binding Decision 2/2023.
note: Six categories, use cases, GDPR articles and the version 2.0 renaming (footnote 3, p. 8) all confirmed; adopted 14 February 2023.

issues.claim: Version 2.0 confirms Chapter V applies to importers caught by Article 3(2) and adds twelve illustrated examples
issues.source_says: Executive summary and section 2.3: criterion 3 is met irrespective of whether the importer is subject to the GDPR under Article 3; the text contains Examples 1 to 12 with illustrations in the Annex, but the document does not say what changed from version 1.0, so 'adds' cannot be checked.

note: Three cumulative criteria (p. 3), direct collection and business-trip employee not transfers (Examples 1 and 8), remote access including screen display as a transfer (para. 16, p. 8) all confirmed.

issues.claim: no reject option where consent is given means no valid consent
issues.source_says: Para. 8 (p. 5): a vast majority of authorities considered the absence of a reject option on any layer with a consent button not in line with valid consent; a few authorities considered they could not retain an infringement because Article 5(3) ePrivacy does not explicitly mention a reject option. Presented as agreed by all.

issues.claim: cookies claimed as essential must be shown to be so
issues.source_says: Para. 28 (p. 7): the responsibility of website owners to maintain cookie lists, provide them to authorities and demonstrate essentiality 'has been discussed'; softer than a settled requirement.

proposed_takeaway: Supervisory authorities agreed a minimum common position on cookie banners: a vast majority hold that no reject option on any layer where consent is sought means no valid consent, pre-ticked boxes are invalid, a reject option hidden as a low-prominence text link is not equivalent to the accept button, deceptive colours and contrast are assessed case by case with unreadable text manifestly non-compliant, cookies claimed as essential must be shown to be so, and withdrawal must be as easy as consent without mandating a specific icon. Where Article 5(3) ePrivacy is breached, subsequent GDPR processing cannot be compliant. The positions apply on top of national ePrivacy law; test each banner against them before relying on the consent.
note: Adopted 17 January 2023 (page date is 18 January). Paras 10, 14, 17-18, 24, 35 and the disclaimer confirm the remaining claims.

issues.claim: found the accept-or-leave choice unfair under Article 5(1)(a)
issues.source_says: Paras 226-232 (pp. 57-58): the fairness infringement rests on Meta presenting its service in a misleading manner and misrepresenting the legal basis, leaving users in the dark; the take-it-or-leave-it situation is cited in para. 231 as a factor that intensifies the imbalance, not as the unfair act itself.

issues.claim: the position later enforced EEA-wide in Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023
issues.source_says: Not in the document.

proposed_takeaway: Meta Platforms Ireland cannot rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR for behavioural advertising on Facebook, because such advertising is objectively not necessary for the performance of the contract and users cannot be taken to expect it from a brief mention in the terms. The EDPB also confirmed infringements of Articles 12 and 13 for unclear information on processing operations and legal bases, found an additional breach of the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) for presenting the service in a misleading way that left users with a take-it-or-leave-it choice, instructed the Irish SA to impose a fine and required compliance within three months of the final decision. Adopted on 5 December 2022, the decision sets the position later enforced EEA-wide in Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023.
note: Paras 484, 489, 493-494, 502 and 509 confirm the Article 6(1) finding, the fairness finding, the three-month orders and the fine instructions; 'brief mention' is at para. 125 area (p. 37).

issues.claim: found the binary accept-or-delete choice unfair
issues.source_says: Paras 455-456 and the fairness analysis: the additional Article 5(1)(a) infringement rests on misleading presentation and misrepresentation of the legal basis; the accept-or-delete-account binary choice (para. 30, p. 9) and the take-it-or-leave-it situation (p. 52) are context that intensifies the imbalance, not the unfair act itself.

issues.claim: it mirrors Binding Decision 3/2022 on Facebook, and both were extended EEA-wide by Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023
issues.source_says: Not in the document; the decision refers to Facebook services only for factual similarities.

proposed_takeaway: Meta Platforms Ireland cannot rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR for behavioural advertising on Instagram: the processing is not a core part of the contract, is objectively unnecessary for its performance and falls outside users' reasonable expectations under the Terms of Use. The EDPB upheld infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13(1)(c) for failing to give meaningful information on processing operations and legal bases, found an additional breach of the fairness principle for presenting the service in a misleading way that left users with an accept-or-delete choice, instructed the Irish SA to impose a fine and set a three-month compliance deadline. Adopted on 5 December 2022, it mirrors Binding Decision 3/2022 on Facebook, and both were extended EEA-wide by Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023.
note: Paras 128-129, 451, 456, 459-460 and 468 confirm the substantive findings, the three-month orders and the fine instruction.

issues.claim: The statement was overtaken by Opinion 5/2023 and by the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision of 10 July 2023
issues.source_says: Not in the document (later events).

note: 25 March agreement, 'positive first step', no legal framework, Schrems II of 16 July 2020 and the three examination points (pp. 1-2) all confirmed; adopted 6 April 2022.

issues.claim: complements the general notification guidance now found in Guidelines 9/2022
issues.source_says: Para. 3 (p. 5): the document complements WP29 Guidelines WP250; Guidelines 9/2022 postdate it and are not mentioned.

note: Version 2.0 adopted 14 December 2021. Eighteen cases in six sections (ransomware, data exfiltration, internal human risk, lost or stolen devices and paper, mispostal, social engineering), fictitious but typical cases, controller audience and the changed-circumstances warning (para. 14) all confirmed; Cases 17 and 18 merge risk assessment, mitigation and obligations into one heading.

issues.claim: approved by the plenary on 14 December 2021
issues.source_says: The report is dated November 2021 (cover) and states that it does not reflect the official opinion of the EDPB and does not bind the EDPB (p. 2); nothing in the text records plenary approval or that date. Only the country questionnaires were approved by the EDPB (p. 4).

issues.claim: transfer impact assessment under Recommendations 01/2020
issues.source_says: The study cites Recommendations 02/2020 on the European Essential Guarantees but not Recommendations 01/2020; the reader action is grounded in the wider EDPB framework, not the study.

proposed_takeaway: Government access to personal data in China, India and Russia is subject to few effective limits: the study finds vague national security concepts, oversight that is absent or internal only, limited remedies for data subjects and, for China, no substantial protection against state access at all, with Russian intelligence agencies described as virtually unrestricted. Commissioned by the EDPB from external researchers and delivered as a final report in November 2021, it carries the authors' views rather than an EDPB position. Use it as documented, publicly available evidence in a transfer impact assessment under Recommendations 01/2020 whenever an exporter sends data to any of the three countries.
note: Prepared by Milieu with KU Leuven researchers under contract EDPS/2019/02-13; substantive country findings confirmed in the executive summary (pp. 4-5).

issues.claim: which subsequently adopted the adequacy decision
issues.source_says: The opinion (24 September 2021) predates the Commission decision and does not address it; this is a wider-world fact, not a claim in the document.

note: Paras 6, 10, 12, 13, 14, 21 (pp. 5 to 7) and para 25 support every substantive point: numerous similarities, binding force of Notification No 2021-1, pseudonymised-data exemptions from data subject rights and retention, no general right to withdraw consent, onward transfers on consent without risk information, unclear national security onward transfers and intelligence sharing. 'Conditions its support' is a fair gloss of the request that the Commission address the concerns and monitor them.

issues.claim: The decision binds the Irish authority and WhatsApp Ireland.
issues.source_says: Para 431 (p. 88): 'This binding decision is addressed to the IE SA and the CSAs. The IE SA shall adopt its final decision on the basis of this binding decision pursuant to Article 65(6) GDPR.' Article 65(2) makes it binding on the lead and concerned supervisory authorities; WhatsApp Ireland is bound by the Irish final decision, not by the EDPB decision itself.

issues.claim: to treat the output of the lossy hashing of non-users' phone numbers as pseudonymised personal data within Article 14
issues.source_says: Para 427 (p. 86): the EDPB 'concludes that the table of lossy hashes together with the associated users' phone numbers as Non-User List constitutes personal data' and (p. 87) extends the Article 14 infringement to the Non-User Lists. 'Pseudonymised' was the characterisation used by the FR, NL and IT SAs in their objections (paras 80, 99, 112), not the EDPB's own operative finding.

issues.claim: 30–50 million euro range
issues.source_says: Para 340 (p. 59): the IE SA proposed a fine 'within the range of 30 million - 50 million euro'; the figure is right, but the dash should be replaced under the no-dash rule.

proposed_takeaway: WhatsApp Ireland's privacy notices infringed the transparency duties in Articles 12 to 14 GDPR, and the EDPB, resolving objections from several supervisory authorities, instructed the Irish Data Protection Commission to add an infringement of Article 13(1)(d) because legitimate interests were not tied to specific processing operations, to treat the table of lossy hashes of non-users' phone numbers held with associated users' numbers as personal data and extend the Article 14 infringement to it, and to reassess the fine upwards from the 30 to 50 million euro range in its draft. The decision binds the Irish authority and the concerned supervisory authorities; WhatsApp Ireland is bound by the Irish final decision adopted on its basis. Read it as the benchmark for how granular a legitimate-interests description and a non-user notice must be.
note: Also confirmed: objections came from DE, IT, PL, FR, HU, NL and PT SAs; para 57 to 59 ground the Article 13(1)(d) finding in the lack of specific information per processing operation; paras 423 to 424 instruct a higher fine. The second file is a one-line corrigendum to the DPC's final decision, not the EDPB decision.

issues.claim: processing for improvement, personalisation or profiling needs consent under Article 6(1)(a)
issues.source_says: Para 86 (p. 32): personalisation within a contractual relationship, as part of a service explicitly requested by the user and limited to what is strictly necessary, may rest on Article 6(1)(b). Para 87: otherwise consent under Article 6(1)(a) is 'in principle' the appropriate basis; para 88: advertising profiling always needs consent; para 80: improvement cannot rest on Article 6(1)(b).

issues.claim: data captured through accidental activation has no legal basis and must be deleted
issues.source_says: Para 30 (p. 13): it is 'highly unlikely' that an Article 5(3) exception or valid consent applies; controllers who become aware of accidental processing 'should verify that there is a valid legal basis for each purpose', otherwise the data 'should be deleted'.

proposed_takeaway: Virtual voice assistants fall under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive as well as the GDPR: storing or accessing data on the device requires prior consent unless strictly necessary to perform a service the user requested, and processing for model improvement, advertising profiling or personalisation beyond the requested service needs, in principle, consent under Article 6(1)(a). Voice recordings are inherently biometric data and fall under Article 9 when used to identify a person, data captured through accidental activation is very unlikely to have a legal basis and should be deleted unless one can be shown, and indefinite retention breaches storage limitation. The guidelines apply to VVA providers, designers, application developers, device manufacturers and integrators. Map the roles in your VVA ecosystem and build voice-based ways to exercise access and erasure.
note: Version 2.0 adopted 7 July 2021 after public consultation. Actors listed in para 15 are provider/designer, application developer, integrator (manufacturer of connected objects), owner and user. Para 31 says voice data is inherently biometric and Article 9 applies when processed for unique identification.

File is Version 2.1 (minor corrections, 20 September 2022) of the text adopted 7 July 2021. Para 40 lists essential means (type of data, duration, categories of recipients and data subjects); executive summary and paras 152 to 153 confirm functional and autonomous concepts, inextricably linked converging decisions, contract not merely restating the GDPR, and prior specific or general written authorisation of sub-processors.

issues.claim: document every step as the transfer impact assessment
issues.source_says: The recommendations require exporters to document the assessment and each step thoroughly (executive summary pp. 4 to 5) but never use the term 'transfer impact assessment'.

note: Six steps match the executive summary and section headings; para 46 lists 'relevant, objective, reliable, verifiable and publicly available or otherwise accessible information'; para 47 says absence of prior requests 'can never be considered, by itself, as a decisive factor'; Annex 2 Use Cases 1 to 5 cover encryption with keys held by the exporter or a trusted EEA entity, pseudonymisation, and split or multi-party processing. Version 2.0 adopted 18 June 2021 after consultation.

Executive summary pp. 2 to 3 and paras 30 to 35, 44 to 48: welcome risk-based approach; general ban on automated recognition of human features in publicly accessible spaces; prohibit any type of social scoring including by private companies; ban emotion inference except well-specified health or research use cases; GDPR and EUDPR compliance as precondition for CE-marked market entry; DPAs as national supervisory authorities under Article 59 of the proposal. Adopted 18 June 2021.

Paras 5 to 12 match: consent 'appears to be the sole appropriate legal basis'; Article 6(1)(b) excluded because storage is only useful for a potential next transaction; 6(1)(c), (d) and (e) excluded; legitimate interest fails on necessity and on the balancing test given highly personal financial data and reasonable expectations; consent via non-pre-ticked checkbox, distinct from terms of service, not a condition of the transaction; withdrawal must lead to effective deletion. Footnote 2 excludes payment institutions, public authorities and recurring subscription payments, which the takeaway omits without being misleading.

issues.claim: Member States and Union bodies should review international agreements
issues.source_says: The statement recalls Article 96 GDPR and Article 61 LED, which concern agreements concluded by Member States, and 'invites the Member States to assess and, where necessary, review their international agreements' (p. 1). Union bodies are not addressed.

issues.claim: check that each carries enforceable rights and effective remedies
issues.source_says: The statement itself only asks for alignment with the GDPR, the LED, CJEU case law and EDPB guidance, pointing to Guidelines 2/2020 for the safeguards; the specific wording comes from those guidelines and Article 46 GDPR, not from the statement.

proposed_takeaway: Member States should review international agreements involving transfers of personal data that were concluded before 24 May 2016 (GDPR) or 6 May 2016 (LED), in fields such as taxation, social security, mutual legal assistance and police cooperation, and align them with Chapter V GDPR, the LED and the Schrems II judgment of 16 July 2020. The statement points to Guidelines 2/2020 on transfers between EEA and non-EEA public authorities for the safeguards required in legally binding instruments, and offers the assistance of the national supervisory authorities. Public-sector practitioners should inventory such agreements and check that each carries enforceable rights and effective remedies.
note: Dates, fields, Schrems II reference (16 July 2020, C-311/18), Guidelines 2/2020 and the offer of SA assistance (Article 51 GDPR, Article 41 LED) are all confirmed.

issues.claim: The UK Data Protection Act 2018 provides, in principle, a level of protection for law enforcement data essentially equivalent to the Law Enforcement Directive
issues.source_says: The opinion does not give a global equivalence verdict. Para 5 (p. 4-5) finds strong alignment on core provisions (concepts, lawfulness, purpose limitation, data quality, retention, security, transparency, special categories, automated decisions); para 7 (p. 5) and para 48 (p. 12) say specifically that Chapter 5 of Part 3 DPA 2018 (onward transfers from UK law enforcement to third countries) provides in principle an essentially equivalent level of protection; para 20 (p. 7) says the EDPB identified many aspects as essentially equivalent and focused on the areas of greatest concern.

proposed_takeaway: The EDPB finds strong alignment between the UK Data Protection Act 2018 and the Law Enforcement Directive on lawfulness, purpose limitation, data quality, special categories and automated decisions, and finds the UK rules on onward transfers from law enforcement authorities essentially equivalent in principle. It asks the Commission to address onward transfers based on UK-only adequacy findings, national security access including certificates that restrict data protection duties, the independence of judicial commissioners, and the effect of the UK-US CLOUD Act agreement, and it welcomes the four-year sunset clause. Addressed to the Commission on 13 April 2021; relevant to competent authorities sharing data with UK law enforcement bodies rather than to private controllers.
note: All other claims confirmed: onward transfers on UK adequacy regulations (paras 8, 49-51), section 79 certificates limiting Chapters 3 and 4 of Part 3 DPA 2018 (paras 38-41), judicial commissioners' independence (paras 60-63), CLOUD Act (paras 10, 52), sunset clause of four years welcomed (paras 24, 27). Version 1.1 of 6 July 2021 is a formatting change only.

issues.claim: Version 2.0 of 13 April 2021 is final
issues.source_says: Version history (p. 2): version 2.0 of 13 April 2021 is the adoption after public consultation, but a version 2.1 of 7 July 2021 follows, amending references to Guidelines 07/2020. The current text is 2.1.

proposed_takeaway: Social media providers and targeters are generally joint controllers for targeting: the targeter chooses the audience criteria and the message, the platform decides which data and criteria are available, so an Article 26 arrangement is required. Article 6(1)(b) cannot support online advertising; legitimate interests requires the three cumulative conditions, and consent is needed for tracking-based profiling and wherever Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive applies to cookies. Telling users merely that data is used for advertising is not transparent enough, inferred special category data rarely benefits from an Article 9(2) exception, and targeting of vulnerable groups calls for a DPIA. Version 2.0 of 13 April 2021 is the final text after consultation; version 2.1 of 7 July 2021 only amended references.
note: Substantive claims confirmed: joint controllership (section 4.5 and 5.x roles), Article 6(1)(b) rejected for both platform and targeter (p. 16-17), three cumulative conditions for Article 6(1)(f) (p. 17), Article 5(3) ePrivacy (section 5.3 and 5.4), 'advertising' alone not enough (section 6, p. 26), manifestly-made-public exception and inferred data (section 8.2), DPIA for vulnerable people (section 7).

issues.claim: Council's negotiating mandate of 10 February 2021
issues.source_says: The statement refers to 'the agreed negotiation mandate adopted by the Council' (p. 1) without giving its date.

note: Retention (p. 1-2), cookie walls and fair alternatives (p. 3), further processing on compatibility (p. 4), overly broad exceptions in Articles 6(1)(c), 6b(1)(e), 6b(1)(f) and 6c (p. 2), and GDPR supervisory authorities plus Chapter VII cooperation and consistency (p. 4) all confirmed.

issues.claim: worked cases on pay-as-you-drive insurance, rental, eCall and accident research
issues.source_says: Section 3 (p. 26-36) contains case studies on provision of a service by a third party (3.1: pay-as-you-drive insurance and 3.1.2 renting and booking a parking space), eCall (3.2), accidentology studies (3.3) and tackling auto theft (3.4). There is no vehicle rental case; the only 'renting' case is parking-space booking.

proposed_takeaway: Most data processed in and around a connected vehicle is personal data, since it can be linked to the driver, owner or passengers, and Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive applies to storing or accessing information on the vehicle, so consent is required unless the access is strictly necessary for a service the user requested. Location, biometric and offence-related data get special treatment: minimise location data, keep biometrics local and encrypted with a non-biometric alternative, and process offence-related data locally under the user's control. Manufacturers, service providers, insurers, dealers, fleet managers and telecom operators are addressed, with worked cases on pay-as-you-drive insurance, parking booking, eCall, accident research and vehicle theft. Version 2.0 of 9 March 2021 is final; prefer local processing and run a DPIA.
note: Personal data (para 3), Article 5(3) and exemptions (paras 12-18), three special data categories (paras 62-69), addressees (para 30), DPIA (para 82) and local processing (section 2.4.1) all confirmed.

issues.claim: Addressed to the Commission in January 2021
issues.source_says: The text carries no adoption date; it records the Commission's request of 12 November 2020 (para 9). The January 2021 date comes from the entry metadata, not the text.

note: Welcomed as a strong accountability tool (para 15); scope, Article 3(2) processors and interplay with transfer SCCs (paras 25-28); docking clause procedure (para 35); controller chooses the auditor (para 43); delete cost references (para 44); annexes with absolute clarity (para 57). All confirmed.

issues.claim: importers already subject to the GDPR under Article 3(2) should be excluded
issues.source_says: Paras 27-30 (p. 9): the EDPB and EDPS understand that the draft decision already does not cover transfers to importers subject to the GDPR under Article 3(2), and recommend the Commission clarify that this concerns only the scope of the decision, not the notion of transfer, and rephrase Article 1(1). It is a request for clarification, not a demand for exclusion.

proposed_takeaway: The draft Article 46 SCCs reinforce protection for data subjects through four modules, a docking clause and clauses on third-country law and government access requests, but the EDPB and EDPS require changes: the assessment of third-country law must rest on objective factors rather than the likelihood of access or the absence of past requests, notification of access requests must precede any response, the processor-to-controller module needs the Article 28 processor obligations and the processor-to-processor module must reflect Article 28(4), and the Commission should clarify that importers already subject to the GDPR under Article 3(2) fall outside the decision. The SCCs must be used with Recommendations 01/2020 on supplementary measures. Addressed to the Commission in January 2021; the transfer impact assessment stays with the exporter.

issues.claim: The guidance on supplementary measures it promised became Recommendations 01/2020

proposed_takeaway: The judgment of 16 July 2020 invalidates the Privacy Shield with immediate effect and no grace period, while standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules remain valid only where the exporter and importer have assessed, case by case, that the law of the destination country allows an essentially equivalent level of protection, adding supplementary measures where it does not. Article 49 derogations are available but cannot become the rule, and an exporter that finds no adequate safeguards must suspend the transfer or, if it intends to keep transferring, notify its supervisory authority. Addressed to controllers and processors exporting data. The guidance on supplementary measures it promised became Recommendations 01/2020, which now carries the operational detail.

issues.claim: document the balancing
issues.source_says: Not stated in those words; the guidelines require the search engine provider to be able to demonstrate overriding legitimate grounds (paras 31-32, 71). Reasonable practical inference.

proposed_takeaway: A data subject may ask a search engine provider to delist results returned for a search on their name on any of the six grounds in Article 17(1) GDPR, and the provider may refuse under the five exemptions in Article 17(3). Delisting removes the link from name-based results only; the content stays on the source website and the request does not erase it there. Search engine operators should test each request against the grounds and then the exemptions, and be able to demonstrate the balancing. Part 1 covers the grounds and exemptions; criteria for handling complaints about refusals are announced for a supplementary appendix.

issues.claim: Most derogations cover only occasional, non-repetitive transfers
issues.source_says: Pages 4-5: recital 111 limits only the contract and legal claims derogations (Art 49(1)(b), (c), (e)) to 'occasional' transfers and the compelling legitimate interests ground to 'not repetitive' transfers; the consent, public interest, vital interests and register derogations ((a), (d), (f), (g)) carry no such express limit, though all must be read as exceptions.

proposed_takeaway: Article 49 derogations are exceptions to be interpreted restrictively so that the exception does not become the rule: an exporter must first look for an adequacy decision under Article 45, then appropriate safeguards under Article 46, and only then a derogation. The contract and legal claims derogations cover only occasional transfers, so a systematic flow within a stable business relationship cannot rest on them, and the compelling legitimate interests ground is a last resort limited to non-repetitive transfers of a limited number of data subjects, with safeguards and notification to the supervisory authority. Exporters should document why Articles 45 and 46 were unavailable before relying on a derogation.
note: Adopted 25 May 2018. Layered approach, restrictive reading, stable-relationship example, last resort, limited number of data subjects and duty to inform the SA all confirmed.

issues.claim: to train or ground a generative AI model
issues.source_says: Executive summary and paras 1-3: the guidelines cover scraping to train, and where relevant fine-tune, generative AI models. Grounding (retrieval at inference time) is not addressed anywhere in the text.

issues.claim: Consultation runs to 30 October 2026
issues.source_says: The document records only 'Version 1.0, 07 July 2026, adoption of the guidelines for public consultation'; no closing date is given.

proposed_takeaway: Scraping the web for personal data to train or fine-tune a generative AI model is processing under the GDPR from the moment of collection, so the scraper needs a legal basis (in practice legitimate interests under the three-step test), purpose limitation and transparency, with the Article 14(5)(b) relief from individual notice only where informing people is impossible or disproportionate and public information is given instead. Controllers should scrape from reliable sources, respect machine-readable opt-outs, record timestamps and provenance, filter and validate data before training, and treat special category data as prohibited unless an Article 9(2) exception applies alongside the Article 6 basis. Consultation runs to 30 October 2026; read it with Opinion 28/2024 on AI models.
